title: Hi-Tec Hiking Boots on Kenyan Trails: Where a Budget British Brand Holds Up, and Where It Doesn't
meta_title: Hi-Tec Hiking Boots in Kenya: 3 Affordable Models Compared
meta_description: Hi-Tec hiking boots in Kenya: which Altitude and Ravus models suit local trails, how Dri-Tec and sizing work, and what to check on a thrifted pair.
excerpt: Hi-Tec hiking boots are light, roomy and good value for day hikes around Nairobi. Here is which models suit Kenyan trails, how they fit and what to check on a second-hand pair.
content:
Hi-Tec hiking boots are a sensible pick for Kenyan day hikes such as Ngong Hills, Hell's Gate and Ol Donyo Sabuk. They are light, come in roomy and extra-wide fits, and most waterproof models use the brand's own Dri-Tec membrane. They are less suited to heavy packs on Mt Kenya scree, where stiffer boots support you better.

The catch is that Hi-Tec has made everything from squash shoes to uniform boots, so a pair on a rail in Nairobi may be a real walking boot or a casual lookalike. Below: which models are built for trails, how Dri-Tec compares with Gore-Tex, how they fit, and what to check on a second-hand pair.

Quick Facts

  • Origin: Hi-Tec was founded in 1974 by Frank van Wezel in Shoeburyness, Essex, England, starting with a lightweight squash shoe.
  • Hiking roots: the brand says its 1978 Sierra sneaker, launched in the USA, was the first lightweight hiking boot.
  • Ownership: Cherokee Inc. (later Apex Global Brands) bought Hi-Tec in 2016; Galaxy Universal acquired Apex in 2021.
  • Waterproofing: most WP or "I WP" models use Dri-Tec, Hi-Tec's own breathable membrane, rather than Gore-Tex.
  • Fit: the Altitude VI I WP comes in medium and extra-wide widths; the Ravus 2.0 WP has extra forefoot volume.
  • Best Kenyan use: Hi-Tec hiking boots suit day hikes and light trails such as Karura, Ngong Hills, Hell's Gate and Kilimambogo.

Is Hi-Tec a Good Brand for Hiking in Kenya?

Hi-Tec is a good brand for everyday hiking in Kenya if you want a light, comfortable boot at a fair price. It is a value brand rather than a mountaineering specialist, so judge each pair by its model line, not by the logo alone.

Its early fame came from sports shoes such as the 1981 Silver Shadow runner, while its American arm launched the Sierra sneaker in 1978 and later the Magnum duty boot.

That history explains the feel of modern Hi-Tec hiking boots: trainer-like comfort, soft midsoles, padded collars and lighter uppers, with many models using the V-LITE lightweight build introduced in 2007. On a Saturday walk in the Ngong Hills, that comfort matters more than stiff support.

For the full timeline, see Hi-Tec's brand history page; our round-up of hiking boot brands for Kenya compares it with Lowa, Keen, Merrell and Salomon.

Which Hi-Tec Hiking Boots Suit Kenyan Trails?

The Altitude and Ravus lines are the Hi-Tec models most worth looking for in Kenya. The Altitude is a leather mid boot for rougher ground; the Ravus is a lighter fabric boot for dry, well-made paths. V-Lite models sit between the two.

Altitude VI I WP: the leather all-rounder

The Altitude is the classic among Hi-Tec hiking boots, and the sixth version is the one you are most likely to find. On Hi-Tec's official Altitude VI I WP page, the upper is waterproof leather treated with i-shield to resist water, dirt and stains. Inside sits a Dri-Tec membrane with a micro-fleece lining, an OrthoLite Impressions insole and a moulded EVA heel cradle with arch support.

Underneath, a CMEVA midsole absorbs impact and a Michelin rubber outsole gives grip on mixed surfaces. Rustproof lacing hardware pays off in Kenya's wet months, and leather copes with the sharp lava rock on Longonot's rim better than the mesh on lighter Hi-Tec hiking boots.

Ravus 2.0 WP: the light fabric option

The Ravus 2.0 WP swaps leather for a one-piece V-LITE soft-shell upper with welded overlays, still backed by a Dri-Tec membrane. It has an EVA midsole, an M-D Traction rubber outsole, ghillie lacing and a gusseted tongue that keeps grit out. The extra forefoot volume suits broad feet, and the lighter build feels closer to a trail shoe on long, dry walks such as the gravel road into Hell's Gate.

Are Hi-Tec Boots Waterproof Enough for Kenya's Rains?

Waterproof Hi-Tec hiking boots keep feet dry through puddles, wet grass and a few hours of rain, which covers most Kenyan day hikes. Dri-Tec is the brand's own membrane, so it is not the same as Gore-Tex, and older pairs can lose their seal.

Check the name first. Hi-Tec hiking boots labelled WP or I WP have a waterproof lining; a plain model may only be water-resistant suede. In the short rains (roughly October to December) and long rains (about March to May), forest tracks in the Aberdares will soak a non-waterproof boot quickly.

A membrane cannot stop water pouring in over the top, so for bog on Elephant Hill add waterproof leg gaiters, and merino wool hiking socks that stay warm when damp. If you hike through the wettest weeks often, a Gore-Tex boot such as the Lowa Renegade GTX Mid is the more durable choice.

How Do Hi-Tec Hiking Boots Fit?

Hi-Tec boots generally fit true to size with a roomy toe box that suits wide feet. The Altitude VI I WP is offered in medium and extra-wide widths, and the Ravus 2.0 WP adds extra forefoot volume.

Most Hi-Tec hiking boots carry UK, EU and US sizes on the tongue label; go by the EU or centimetre figure, since UK and US numbers differ by about one size. Try boots in the afternoon, in your hiking socks, and check you can fit a finger behind your heel with the boot unlaced.

Narrow feet may find the heel lifts on steep climbs such as Ol Donyo Sabuk; a thicker sock or firmer insole usually fixes that. For conversions, see our guide to hiking boot sizes in Kenya.

What Should You Check on a Second-Hand Hi-Tec Pair in Nairobi?

Hi-Tec sold in huge numbers on British and European high streets, so thrifted pairs reach Nairobi regularly. Second-hand Hi-Tec hiking boots can give several seasons of day hikes for far less than new, provided the sole and lining are sound.

The EVA-type midsoles Hi-Tec uses are light and soft but slowly compress with use, so judge the midsole first on any pre-owned pair. Work through these checks before you buy:

  1. Press your thumb into the midsole at the heel. It should spring back; deep creases that stay flat mean the cushioning is spent.
  2. Look along the edge where the sole meets the upper, especially at the toe. Any gap or lifting rubber is hard to repair well.
  3. Check the tread depth under the ball of the foot and the heel. Lugs worn smooth will slip on the dusty Ngong ridge and on wet rock.
  4. Feel inside the heel for torn lining or exposed foam, which causes blisters within a few kilometres.
  5. Find the size label and the WP or Dri-Tec marking so you know the boot is the waterproof version.
  6. Flex the boot. Leather should bend without cracking across the toe crease.

How can you tell a genuine Hi-Tec boot?

Genuine Hi-Tec hiking boots usually have a size label with a product code inside the tongue, even stitching, a moulded outsole logo and branded insoles such as OrthoLite on recent models. Flimsy soles, crooked logos and missing labels are warning signs, though none of these is proof on its own.

How Do Hi-Tec Boots Compare With Other Boots We Stock?

Hi-Tec hiking boots sit in the light, comfortable middle of the market, trading some stiffness and long-term durability for comfort straight out of the box.

The Quechua Forclaz 500 High waterproof boot is the closest rival: light, waterproof and cut higher at the ankle. The Keen Targhee Mid waterproof boot shares the Ravus's wide toe box, with deeper lugs for mud. The Lowa Renegade, with Gore-Tex and a firmer chassis, is the step up for Mt Kenya or overnight loads.

Where do Hi-Tec hiking boots make the most sense? On the trails most people around Nairobi walk every month: the Ngong ridge, Hell's Gate, Kilimambogo and the forest loops of Karura and Oloolua. Our Ngong Hills hike guide is a good test walk for any new pair.

Pro Tips: Making Hi-Tec Hiking Boots Last

  • Rinse and dry slowly: wash off black cotton soil the same day and dry boots in the shade, never by a jiko.
  • Re-proof: wax leather Altitudes and spray fabric Ravus models with DWR.
  • Swap the insole: a fresh insole revives thrifted Hi-Tec hiking boots whose upper and sole are still good.
  • Break them in: walk 2-3 short outings before a long hike like Longonot.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Hi-Tec hiking boots any good?

Hi-Tec walking boots are good value for day hikes and light trails. Models such as the Altitude VI I WP combine a leather upper, Dri-Tec membrane and Michelin rubber sole, which handles Ngong Hills, Hell's Gate and Kilimambogo comfortably. They are softer and less supportive than premium mountain boots, so they are not the first pick for heavy loads or long Mt Kenya treks.

Is Dri-Tec as good as Gore-Tex?

Dri-Tec is Hi-Tec's own waterproof, breathable membrane, and it keeps feet dry through puddles, wet grass and rain showers on most day hikes. Gore-Tex has a longer track record and usually stays waterproof for longer under heavy use. If you hike every rainy weekend or plan multi-day treks, a Gore-Tex boot is worth the extra cost.

Do Hi-Tec boots run big or small?

Hi-Tec hiking boots usually run true to size, with a roomy toe box that suits wide feet. If your feet are narrow, your heel may lift on steep climbs, so try a thicker hiking sock or a firmer insole, and always fit boots with the socks you plan to hike in.

Can I climb Mt Kenya in Hi-Tec hiking boots?

Hi-Tec Altitude boots can manage Point Lenana in the dry seasons for a fit hiker carrying only a light daypack. The softer midsole gives less support on loose scree and the boot is less warm on summit night. For a first Mt Kenya climb, a stiffer, fully waterproof boot such as the Lowa Renegade GTX is the safer choice.

How long do Hi-Tec hiking boots last?

Most Hi-Tec boots last a few seasons of regular day hikes, depending on terrain, body weight and care. The EVA-type midsole usually wears out before the upper, so cushioning goes flat and the tread smooths off. Cleaning off mud, slow drying and re-proofing all help a pair last longer.

Final Thoughts

Think of Hi-Tec as the dependable middle of the boot rack. An Altitude or Ravus with a firm midsole and a deep tread will carry you round the ridges, gorges and forests near Nairobi in comfort, and buying thrifted makes Hi-Tec hiking boots even more affordable. Save the stiffer Gore-Tex boots for Mt Kenya and heavy packs.
